# **Assisted and Auto Bus Planning in Full-Chip Layout**

**Abstract**

We present new tools for physical design of full-chip interconnect. Instead of planning nets one at a time, we model the interconnect in terms of groups of nets, each denoted as a *bus*. The *bus* concept is similar to what has been used in lead processor designs at Intel, e.g., Pentium4TM and ItaniumTM. Our tools generate topologies which are used to design the interconnect in a top-down and hierarchical approach without the need for bottom-up terminals.

In *assisted bus planning*, we provide a number of alternate topologies for the designer to view and choose among. The designer can influence what kinds of topologies are created in an interactive flow. Topologies are generated automatically to connect to lower level blocks/cells at a given depth. Once a topology is chosen, the designer can further customize all relevant parameters of the topology. In *auto bus planning*, power grid and pre-placed obstacles on the chip are taken into account efficiently through a new track sharing technique. This enables very quick timing feedback to RTL design based on accurate physical design information.

Both assisted and auto bus planning techniques are implemented in our full-chip layout tool, Galaxy, and are currently being used by various design teams. Studies demonstrate significant productivity gains compared to designing buses manually using a layout editor: Auto bus planning has been used in Manzano project to plan almost all of the full-chip interconnect and helped reduce the design cycle from RTL to RCEXT down to a couple of days. It is currently under experimentation for use in Tejas and CedarMill mega-blocks as well as full-chip design. Assisted bus planning has been used in Tanglewood to plan all buses inside the core and to manage ongoing RTL changes and ECOs.

1. **Introduction**

Planning full-chip interconnect is one of the most complex tasks in the design of lead processors at Intel. In this paper, we present a set of new tools, as part of our full-chip layout design tool Galaxy, which aim to increase the productivity of a designer in achieving this task.

**Design Objectives**: Interconnect planning is one of the most important tasks in the design of microprocessors. It has a major impact on not only performance and die-size of the chip, but also tape-out deadlines and time to market. The two main goals of interconnect planning during layout design of a chip are: 1\) Identify and address floor-plan congestion due to wiring early on, 2\) Ensure that each critical signal follows a good and predictable path on the chip to connect its driver to its receivers. This is important for speedy convergence of timing performance of the chip. 

Our challenges in achieving these objectives are as follows: 1\) Plan major interconnect before bottom-up data is available, 2\) Provide quick and accurate floor-plan feedback to designers based on interconnect, 3\) Plan full-chip interconnect in presence of hierarchy down to lowest-level building blocks (FUB or EBB). 4\) Capture designer’s decisions and intent on interconnect routes and preserve them throughout design iterations.

**Bus Planning In Galaxy**: Traditionally, Intel designers coped with interconnect planning using the concept of a “bus”. Our previous generation full-chip layout tool, ChPPR, provides a rich set of editing capabilities that help to create and modify buses to plan the full-chip interconnect.

In Galaxy, we improve on the bus planning capabilities of ChPPR in two major areas:

1) Assisted bus planning: Automatic generation of a set of alternative topologies that ensures that buses connect to a given set of blocks at a given depth of design hierarchy,

2) Auto bus planning: Fast track sharing of topologies that help identify congestion and refine bus plans.

Note that, in addition bus planning, Galaxy also improves manual creation and editing of buses significantly over ChPPR. However, those features are outside the scope of this paper. Please see \[1\] and \[2\] for a description of manual bus planning/editing features in Galaxy.

Our bus planning tool in Galaxy is based on a new model of “bus topology”. This model captures the intent of the designer as to how a bus should be routed in a rough “topology” to connect a driver to its receivers across the full-chip. It does not rely on existence of bottom-up terminals and as such is ideally suited for early and mid-stages of design where bottom-up design data is not available, or is not clean enough for auto-routing. 

In “assisted bus planning” tool set, the designer can quickly cycle through buses in the design and see alternative topologies for planning of each bus. This tool set relieves the designer from having to design a bus by pointing and clicking on the canvas. In addition, it provides controls to guide the customization of a selected topology, e.g., the routing layers used, the playing field of the topology, i.e., how much room it has to move around, on which edge to connect to a block and how much to extend into the block boundary, etc.

In “auto bus planning” tool set, a new track-sharing engine converts bus topologies to wires in order to eliminate overlaps between them. This engine is not as accurate as an auto-router, but in exchange for accuracy, it is very fast in “legalizing” critical buses. This enables designers to make floorplan and bus topology changes very quickly by a rich set of commands to visualize and quantify congestion. After track sharing, most of the full-chip bus wiring is done, which enables accurate RC extraction to identify timing issues early on. Our track-sharing tool is also very accurate in taking into account power grid even before a power grid is fully designed. This ensures that both congestion and timing results provide a high level of confidence to the designer to make informed design decisions early on in the design.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe how components of bus planning flows fit together and briefly describe usage in a design flow. In Section 3, we define bus topology formally and describe how alternative topologies are generated for assisted bus planning. In Section 4, we describe track sharing and other components of auto bus planning. Finally, in Sections 5 and 6, we present results based on usage in Manzano, Nehalem, Tanglewood, Tejas and CedarMill projects and discuss future opportunities. 

2. **Bus Planning Flows**

Figure 1 shows major components of assisted and auto bus planning flows. Note that the user can interact with and control all major tasks in this flow. Detailed descriptions of these tasks will be provided in Sections 3 and 4\.

It is important to note that assisted and auto bus planning flows interact with other important floor-planning tasks. A sample design flow, similar to what is used in Manzano full-chip design, is shown in Figure 2\.

3. **Assisted Bus Planning**

Our purpose in assisted bus planning is to help the designer in choosing an appropriate topology for each bus in the design. Let us start by defining what we mean by a *bus*. 

**Definition: Bus**

We define a bus to be a set of nets with either a similar signal name, or similar connectivity. E.g., nets XPNCOMMIT\[0\] and XPNCOMMIT\[1\] could form a bus named as, say, XPNCOMMIT\[0-1\] and nets P\_TERM\[0\] and N\_TERM\[0\] could be bundled in another bus, say, TERM\_BUS1. We denote a bus without any layout data, i.e., wires/vias, as a *logical bus*. A logical bus is simply a set of nets. A physical bus, on the other hand, is a bus with some layout associated with it.

**Bundling**

The input to assisted bus planning is a logical bus. In the absence of logical buses, we also provide commands to automatically create them based on signal names and connectivity. We denote creation of buses as *bundling*. This enables the designer to jump-start interconnect planning as soon as blocks are placed and a schematic netlist is read in.  Note that the designer has full control on what nets are bundled into buses as shown in Figure 1\.

![][image1]

**Figure 1 Bus planning flows**

**![][image2]**

**Figure 2 Interconnect design flow** 

**Definition: Busterm and busterm generation**

The first step after bundling is determining regions on the layout that the bus needs to connect to. We denote each such target as a *bus-terminal*, or *busterm* for short.  

Busterms are rectangle-shaped objects that can be automatically generated as follows. Let *HBLOCKS* represents the set of blocks at a specified hierarchy depth, where each block has at least one net in the bus that connects to it. Then,

* For each block in HBLOCKS, if the block has a rectangular boundary, a busterm is generated that coincides with its boundary.

* If the block has a non-rectangular boundary, then a busterm is generated for each edge of this block. These busterms are marked to be in an equivalence group in order that the bus plan connects to only one of them. We support two modes of planning: over-the-block and through-the-block. Please see section on topology generation for details.

* If the bus is an I/O bus (i.e., at least one of its nets is an I/O net), then a busterm for the top cell can be optionally created. This busterm coincides with the edge of the cell boundary that is closest to other busterms on this bus. This is useful for bottom-up planning of boundary terminals. For top-down planning, or non-boundary (port) terminal planning, this option can be turned off or overridden by designer to use a different edge.

* Optionally, bottom-up (net) terminals on the bus can be used to generate busterms as follows: all the terminals on each block are clustered according to their layers, locations, connectivity, and terminal equivalence group (TEG) properties. Potentially, there can be multiple busterms per block, if the block has multiple terminals for at least one of the nets on the bus. 

* Designer can manually add or refine busterms for a given bus using convenient commands available with Galaxy’s GUI. 

Busterm generation supports mixing of manual and automated busterms as well as busterms based on some blocks and busterms based on net terminals for other blocks. 

**Topology generation**

We denote the task of connecting busterms to each other as *topology generation.* The input to topology generation is a set of busterms. The output is a set of alternative *bus topologies,* each of which follows different paths to connect these busterms together. For example, see Figure 3 and Figure 4\. Note that all of these topologies have very few bends (or vias), which is the main premise of topology generation.

A bus topology, or *topo* for short, is defined by a set of *topo segments*, or simply *segments*. Each segment has the following properties/components:

* An orientation (horizontal or vertical) and a range where it can be placed in. The range of a horizontal segment is a vertical interval, \[ymin, ymax\] and vice versa for a vertical segment (See Figure 3).

* Anchors: this is the subset of busterms that this segment needs to connect to. This set can be empty; in which case, the segment is denoted as *floating*.

* Connections: this is a subset of orthogonal segments that this segment needs to connect to with a via. This set can be empty.

Topology generation is influenced by a number of properties on busterms:

* Direction: A busterm may need to be connected only from a specified set of directions, e.g., in case of boundary terminals, or block edges, only North, in case of port terminals, only East or West, etc. Direction properties for block edges, boundary terminals, top-cell boundary and port terminals are determined automatically and the designer can override them.

* Terminal equivalence group (TEG): Among the busterms that belong to a TEG, only one needs to be connected (or anchored to). Feedthroughs can be controlled witha flag: If the value is set to *over-the-block*, then topology segments that anchor to different busterms in a TEG are connected to each other. Otherwise, it is assumed that there is wiring *thru-the-block* to connect these terminals, therefore, the bus segments are left disconnected.

* Leaf-node: Some busterms, e.g., a top-cell edge, are connected with only one segment.

Topologies can be generated based on two algorithms:

* Mixed Steiner /spanning trees, and/or

* Single-trunk and stub based Steiner trees.

Both of these algorithms are designed to meet bus planning needs. Classical Steiner tree generation algorithms assume that nodes of the tree are dimensionless points on a plane. In our algorithms, the major challenge is handling rectangular nodes with TEG and direction properties. We provide options to design topologies with minimum possible jogs vs. largest possible flexibility for topo segments. The number of topologies that are generated for a bus depends on the number, shape and relative position of busterms. The details of these algorithms are outside the scope of this paper and will be presented elsewhere.

**![][image3]**

**Figure 3 Busterms and sample bus topologies for three buses. Note that ranges on each topology segment are depicted with arrows.**

After a set of topologies is generated, they can be sorted based on a number of criteria: 

* Number of jogs/vias, 

* Wirelength, 

* Flexibility (i.e., size of segment ranges) and

* Congestion they see on their path.

Sorting based on congestion requires that each topo segment is assigned a routing layer (see next section). The congestion on the floor-plan also needs to be analyzed on each layer. Cutline module shown in Figure 1 computes the congestion on each natural cutline on the floorplan. Then each topology is assigned a fitness value based on the congestion it sees on its segments.

**Layer assignment**

So far, the topologies we generated are not associated with any routing layer. In this step, the designer can assign layers to topologies by specifying either:

* A pair of horizontal and vertical layers, or 

* A layer look-up table that maps intervals of wirelength to layer pairs.


  

  **Track assignment** 

In this step, we add symbolic wires to the topologies. In assisted bus planning, symbolic wires for each segment are placed within the segment ranges, without any regard for other topologies or layout. The exact location of wires in a topology segment, within its range, is decided primarily so as to reduce the wirelength. E.g., Figure 5 shows a topology that connects to three blocks and a top-cell edge. It has two segments, one vertical and one horizontal; and their ranges. Note that wires in the horizontal segment are placed in the center of its range, whereas, wires in the vertical segment are “pulled”, i.e., placed closer to the left corner of its range in order to minimize the length of the wires in the horizontal segment. 

**![][image4]**

**Figure 4 Some alternative topologies for a bus**

![][image5]

**Figure 5 A topology after track assignment in assisted bus planning**

**Conversion to layout**

Once the designer is happy with a topology, she can convert it to real layout for further editing, design rule checking and RC extraction. In this step, all the symbolic wires in a topology are converted to real wires (*UdmWire*) and are bundled within a physical bus (*UdmBus*). The range and pull information on each segment are added to the bus as properties to be used during gridding.

**Gridding**

During gridding, wires on each bus segment are snapped on a routing grid defined by the designer. By using the range and pull information generated in the previous step, the wires are ensured to stay within the block boundaries that they need to connect to. 

Note that, up to this step, wires in a bus are not design-rule-correct. The gridding feature in Galaxy can take into account obstacles, like KORs and wires, as well as other buses while finding the nearest routing tracks to snap wires on. Details on gridding features in Galaxy can be found in \[3\] .

4. **Auto Bus Planning**

Auto bus planning provides a set of additional commands on top of those provided by assisted bus planning, in order to “legalize” the topologies, help analyze congestion in the floorplan and get more accurate information on wirelength. Legalization comprises taking the following into account:

* Existing topologies,

* Power grid,

* Layout obstacles, e.g., KORs, pre-routes, etc.

There are two major flows that we provide in auto bus planning: 1\) Dilution based fast track sharing, 2\) Obstacle-aware track sharing.

Both of these flows can be preceded by an optional step that sorts topologies based on congestion in the design. Congestion can be analyzed using only floorplan and netlist information, or topologies and existing layout.

**Dilution based fast track sharing**

This flow is targeted for early stages of design when RTL and floorplan changes are large. The goal is to legalize topologies quickly to provide feedback to the designer on congestion and timing aspects of the floorplan accurately.

In order to take power grid into account efficiently, we employ a design technique practiced by various full-chip designs in the past, denoted as dilution \[4\]. In this technique, exact location of power grid wires is immaterial. Instead, the power grid is taken into account by making sure that in any large enough region, no more routing tracks are used than are available. E.g., assume that we have a repetitive pattern of power grid, where VCC/VSS wires require 20 microns out of every 100 microns. Also assume that we can fit one routing track in every micron (width+spacing). After power grid is embedded, we can only fit 80 signal tracks in this region. Using a diluted spacing between wires, we ensure that buses segments in any region with a size of 100 microns use at most 80 tracks. The designer can specify how much resource needs to be reserved for power grid per layer, e.g. 20% for metal5. The rest of the flow automatically assigns a location to each symbolic topology wire such that it resides in its range and does not overlap any other topology.

Once dilution based track sharing is run, the designer can find out quickly whether and how much congestion exists on the floorplan. We provide commands to visualize congestion and provide query methods to report what buses contribute to congestion in a given area and number of additional tracks needed to accommodate congested buses. Early in the design this information is used to update the floorplan by resizing block edges, moving blocks around and growing the die as necessary \[5\] . The designer can also highlight buses that contribute to congestion and see the layout in context with dimmed colors. This makes it very easy to visualize alternative topologies to get around congestion. 

**Obstacle-aware track sharing**

For mid to late stages of design, when power grid is embedded and layout exists for most buses, nets, we provide a “heavy-duty” version of track sharing, which legalizes topologies with respect to existing obstacles in the design. This takes considerably more run-time than the dilution based flow, however, it ensures that once converted to layout, topologies will not create design rule errors. 

**Track sharing engine**

For track sharing, we designed and implemented a new algorithm that can pack bus topology segments and wires with respect to range constraints. Its objective is to minimize wirelength while maximizing completion, i.e., numbers of buses without DRVs. Range constraints from topologies are processed to take pre-routes and KORs into account. The details of this algorithm are outside the scope of this paper and will be presented elsewhere.

**Gridding**

Once track sharing is done, wires in buses are legal with respect to each other; however, they may be shorting power wires. Gridding legalizes bus wires by snapping them on routing tracks (See Figure 6). In order to ensure that buses stay connected to their blocks, the gridder takes the topology ranges into account and does not change the relative ordering of bus segments. For details, please see \[3\] .

![][image6]

**Figure 6 Track sharing with dilution. (a) Topologies with ranges for three buses. (b) Bus wires after track sharing. (c) Result after gridding. Red rectangles denote VCC/VSS wires.**

5. **Results**

Assisted and auto bus planning features are fully implemented and productized as part of Galaxy.  Figure 7 shows the bus planning GUI in the latest version of Galaxy \[1\] . Here, we will first describe usage in a number of projects and then provide detailed run-time numbers on a suite of test cases we have collected during our interaction with designers in various projects.

**Tanglewood** engineers have made extensive use of assisted bus planning \[6\] . The floorplan of the core, called *SLICE*, is shown in Figure 8\. This represents one processor, which is instantiated multiple times to make up the multi-processor chip. SLICE is designed with a deep hierarchy. At the top-level there are seven partitions. Each partition is called a *BOX*. In decreasing size, these are: C, M, I, F, Q, E and TNC. Each BOX is comprised of a number of sections, which are composed of FUBs. In the case of MBOX, which contains various data paths and M- and D-caches, the hierarchy is even deeper. 

![][image7]

**Figure 7 Bus Planning GUI**

**![][image8]**

**Figure 8 Tanglewood SLICE**

Figure 9 shows busterms and one topology for a bus that flows between M and Q boxes. Note that busterms \#0 and \#1 are lower level blocks in MBOX and busterm \#2 is a lower level block in QBOX. For this bus, there were 11 other topologies that were generated automatically among which the designers chose one. All full-chip buses were planned using assisted bus planning to connect to sections or FUBs two or more levels down. Designers stated that assisted bus planning was *“a fantastic resource to accomplish bus routing rapidly… I have personally used Galaxy topology generator to generate, and re-generate over 100 buses for the Tanglewood project. What a time saver over manual bussing\!" “Galaxy auto-bussing was extremely helpful. I can't imagine how long it would have taken us without this feature*" \[9\] . 

![][image9]

**Figure 9 Busterms and first topology for bus q\_\_mbox\_iss\_ld\_dst1\_q3a\_h\[0-7\] in Tanglewood SLICE. There are 12 topologies generated for this bus.**

Engineers in **Manzano-Xscale** project have been using both assisted and auto bus planning \[5\] . Figure 10 shows the processor core (MZ\_CORE) and full-chip buses. Manzano full-chip designer relied on auto bus planning to generate topologies and analyze congestion after track sharing. Assisted bus planning was used on some buses to choose alternate topologies to resolve congestion on block edges. Early on during the design, when RTL and floor-plan changes were large in magnitude, auto bus planning has been used exclusively to design about 95% of all signal wires without congestion, so that, in a matter of days, RC extraction and timing could be run on the chip with very high confidence. Originally, the flow from a new RTL drop to RC extraction required 5 days due to some manual effort to handhold various tasks in the flow. We have worked with Manzano designers to implement two major enhancements (centering bridging buses on lower metal layers and better snapping on to routing grid) to reduce this effort down to one to two days. Resulting flow is shown in Figure 2\. As RTL and floorplan stabilized, most topologies were re-used from previous iteration and only ECOs were implemented from scratch using assisted and auto bus planning. Resulting buses were also used to generate top-down constraints to drive FUB layout using a place and route tool. 

Designers in the next generation lead-processor design **Nehalem** have piloted bus planning flows with an innovative bottom-up/top-down design \[7\] . They used an early floorplan for IEXEC unit, which has two instances of ICLUST cell. ICLUST has a deep hierarchy of datapaths with as many as 4 levels of cells. They first ran bus planning on the lower-level ICLUST cell on all local buses. Then, they shadowed up resulting buses as obstacles for planning all buses in IEXEC down to lowest-level FUBs in ICLUST. Bus planning flows were able to plan most of the buses. A senior designer using assisted bus planning and manual bus editing features planned remaining buses. At the end of this flow, all nets in the design hierarchy are accounted for and no further planning is required. The total design effort was a couple of designer hours. This compares very favorably to manual bus editing, which the expert designer estimates to be at least 2 days of effort.

Recently, **Tejas** designers have started using assisted bus planning to plan buses through repeater stations (by using extra busterms to direct topologies to repeater stations) and to the vicinity of terminals that exist in their design \[8\] . This is a marked difference to earlier usage of bus planning to plan buses to block boundaries only. So far, they find bus planning to handle most of their buses and save them a lot of time in the process. 

![][image10]

**Figure 10 Buses in Manzano core**

Last but not least, we provide experimental data on a large suite of designs to illustrate scaling performance of major components of bus planning flows (See Table 1). The first column shows number of total nets in the schematic of each design. Second column shows number of logical buses that are generated after auto-bundling. Note that these buses account for all the nets given in the first column. In other words, even non-bus (scalar) nets are bundled and planned as buses. Third column shows the total number of topologies that get generated for all buses. For each bus, an average of 7 topologies are generated. In some cases this number is much higher due to large number of busterms to connect to. Some buses are dangling (one or zero busterms to connect to), in which case the number of topologies is 0\.

The next column gives the run-time, in seconds, of each major component of assisted and auto bus planning flows. The first component is the time it takes to generate all the topologies shown in the previous column for all the buses. This also includes the time it takes to assign wires to each bus, w/o track sharing. Note that in assisted bus planning, it is not a common practice to generate topologies for all buses. Instead, the designer first selects a small set of critical/large buses and then generates the topologies for those. This operation takes on average 6 seconds for 100 buses. This average goes up to as much as 20 seconds, in the case of Banias/aviram, which has a deep hierarchy with standard-cells at the leaf nodes.

The second component of run-time is for the first iteration of track sharing in auto bus planning. At the end of this iteration, each bus has the shortest possible length, however, number of dirty buses is large. The third component shows the run-time for a simple auto bus planning flow. This flow is comprised of 1\) choosing the first topology for each bus after sorting with respect to number of segments 2\) running an internal DRV engine to find dirty buses after track sharing, and 3\) a number of iterations around track sharing to trade off wirelength for reduction in the number of dirty buses (by increasing topology segment ranges). The number of iterations is determined by a number of factors: size of topology segment ranges, number of segments in a given range, etc. 

Finally, the last column shows the number of dirty buses after auto bus planning flow is complete. Note that for larger designs, this number is rather high. However, this is expected as in a realistic flow, scalar nets should be routed with an auto-router rather than bundling them into buses as we have done in this experiment.

6. **Summary and future opportunities**

We have presented assisted and auto bus planning features in Galaxy and how they have been used in various design projects. Our design partners have reported significant productivity gains by using our tools as compared to planning buses manually. Going forward, we are focusing on planning buses to terminals, which may be subject to movement, and keeping topologies unperturbed between iterations of physical integration. Further, we are planning to integrate bus routing with net routing in order to combine the strengths of these two techniques.
